description: Oil just had its worst three days since the pandemic on hopes of an end to the Iran war, and airline stocks exploded. Why did it happen, what does it mean for your gas tank, and who actually won: $10 a day in airlines or $10 a day in oil since the war began?
- 24/7 Wall St.: airline and cruise stock moves, Nov 2 and Nov 4, 2026
- Global Oil Shock tracker: Brent prices and Hormuz shipping
Gas math is a rough rule of thumb (42 gallons per barrel), not a forecast.
Not financial advice. For education only.

segments.vo: Oil just had its worst three days since the pandemic. And airline stocks went absolutely wild.
Brent crude, the world's benchmark oil price, fell about {brent3_pct} in three trading days. The last time oil dropped this hard, this fast? {brent3_last}.

And the next day, the stocks that hate expensive oil exploded. JetBlue was {JBLU_d1_words} in one day. United, {UAL_d1_words}. Delta, {DAL_d1_words}. American, {AAL_d1_words}. Meanwhile the oil fund everybody piles into was {USO_d1_words}.

So why did oil crash? Does this mean cheaper gas for you? And stay to the end, because I'll show you what happened to ten dollars a day in airlines versus ten dollars a day in oil, since the war started. The answer is not what you think.
First, why was oil so expensive in the first place? One word. Iran.

The war with Iran started at the end of February. Then shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow sea lane where a huge share of the world's oil passes, got squeezed hard. Oil climbed for months. Brent hit its 2026 high of {oil_peak} on {oil_peak_date}.

Then, at the start of November, traders started betting on something they hadn't dared to for months. A deal. Hopes for an end to the fighting, and oil flowing again. And when traders change their minds about oil, they don't do it slowly.

scene.source: Charles Schwab; Global Oil Shock tracker

segments.vo: Now here's the part most headlines skip. Why do airlines care so much?

Because jet fuel is one of an airline's biggest costs, often second only to paying its people. When oil falls, every flight gets cheaper to fly overnight. The planes don't change. The tickets don't change. But the profit on each seat does. Cruise lines are the same story. Carnival and Royal Caribbean jumped about five percent when the oil slide started.
And the losers? Anyone who sells oil. Drillers, oil funds, and countries whose budgets run on oil money. The oil giant Exxon was {XOM_d1_words} on the same day.

segments.chapter: What it means for your gas tank
segments.vo: Okay. Your wallet. Does this mean cheaper gas?

A barrel of oil is forty-two gallons. So in theory, every dollar off a barrel takes a bit more than two cents off a gallon. Brent is now around {oil_now}, down from {oil_peak} at the peak. That's about {gas_cents} a gallon in crude costs. On a fifteen-gallon fill-up, about {tank_saving}.

scene.kicker: Peak to now, crude cost per gallon
scene.source: Math: (peak − now) ÷ 42. Brent prices: Yahoo Finance

segments.vo: But here's the twist. Gas stations are quick to raise prices and slow to cut them. Economists even have a name for it. Rockets and feathers. Prices shoot up like a rocket, and float down like a feather. So the savings come. Just slowly.

And if oil went all the way back to sixty dollars, where it sat before the war? That would be about {oil60_cents} less per gallon than today. Roughly {oil60_tank} a tank. Not life-changing. But every single week, for every driver, it adds up to billions.
And now, the moment I promised. Say you put ten dollars every trading day into airlines, through the big airline fund, JETS, starting the first trading day after the war began.
You'd have put in {bt_invested}. Today that's worth {bt_value}. That's {bt_return_words}. And your worst moment? On {bt_dd_date}, you were {bt_dd_words} from your peak.

Now the same ten dollars a day, same start date, in oil itself, through the oil fund USO. You'd have {USO_dca_value}. That's {USO_dca_words}. Exxon? {XOM_dca_value}, {XOM_dca_words}. And a boring S&P 500 fund? {SPY_dca_value}, {SPY_dca_words}. So which bet paid the most, through a whole war? {dca_winner}.

One more twist. Picture the scariest day of the year for oil, April twenty-ninth, the peak. Everybody's panicking. Say you had ten thousand dollars. Bet one: you buy oil, because it's going up forever. Today that's {peakuso_value}. That's {peakuso_change_words}.

scene.kicker: Bought oil at the April peak

segments.vo: Bet two: you buy the thing everyone hated that day. JetBlue. Today that's {peakjblu_value}. That's {peakjblu_change_words}. The crowd was loudest exactly at the top.

scene.label: JetBlue
scene.kicker: Bought airlines at the April peak

segments.vo: So what happens next? We don't predict. But here are three ways this goes.

scene.sub: No predictions. Just what to watch.

segments.vo: One. Deal. A real agreement, ships move freely through Hormuz, and oil keeps sliding. Two. Stall. Talks drag on, and oil bounces around where it is. Three. Snapback. Talks fail, and oil rockets right back up, and the airlines give it all back. Watch the shipping numbers through Hormuz. They'll tell you before the headlines do.
